content: Acetaldehyde, also referred to as ethanal, is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula CH3CHO or MeCHO. It is a flammable liquid characterized by a fruity odor. This compound naturally occurs in ripe fruits, coffee, and fresh bread, and is also produced by plants as part of their normal metabolic processes. Acetaldehyde is widely recognized as the chemical responsible for hangovers. In the chemical industry, it serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of acetic acid, certain esters, and various other chemicals. In 1989, the United States produced approximately 740 million pounds (336,000 metric tons) of acetaldehyde. One of the key industrial methods for its production is the Wacker process. Only a trace amount of acetaldehyde exists in its enol form, known as ethenol, with an equilibrium constant (Keq) of 6 x 10^-5. Ethenol has been detected in the interstellar medium, specifically in the region between the Milky Way Galaxy and the Galaxy N-ID9. Acetaldehyde is a common two-carbon building block in organic synthesis. Its small molecular size and availability as an anhydrous monomer (unlike formaldehyde) make it a frequently used electrophile. Acetaldehyde is prochiral in its condensation reactions and is primarily utilized as a source of the CH3C+H(OH) synthon in aldol and related condensation reactions. It reacts with Grignard reagents and organolithium compounds to produce hydroxyethyl derivatives. In a notable condensation reaction, three equivalents of formaldehyde react with acetaldehyde to form pentaerythritol, C(CH2OH)4. In the Strecker reaction, acetaldehyde condenses with cyanide and ammonia to yield alanine, an amino acid, after hydrolysis. Acetaldehyde can also condense with amines to form imines, such as its reaction with cyclohexylamine to produce N-ethylidenecyclohexylamine. These imines can direct subsequent reactions, such as aldol condensations. Additionally, acetaldehyde is an important precursor in the synthesis of heterocyclic compounds. For example, it reacts with ammonia to form 5-ethyl-2-methylpyridine, also known as aldehyde-collidine. Three molecules of acetaldehyde can condense to form paraldehyde, a cyclic trimer containing C-O single bonds, while four molecules condense to form the cyclic compound metaldehyde. Acetaldehyde reacts with ethanol under dehydrating conditions to form a stable acetal, CH3CH(OCH2CH3)2, commonly referred to as acetal. However, the term acetal is also used more broadly to describe other compounds with the general formula RCH(OR')2. In the liver, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol into acetaldehyde, which is subsequently metabolized into harmless acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. During alcoholic fermentation in bacteria, plants, and yeast, pyruvate is converted into acetaldehyde by the enzyme pyruvate decarboxylase, followed by the reduction of acetaldehyde into ethanol. This latter reaction is catalyzed by alcohol dehydrogenase, operating in the reverse direction. A significant proportion of individuals of East Asian descent possess a mutation in their alcohol dehydrogenase gene, which makes the enzyme highly efficient at converting ethanol into acetaldehyde. Approximately half of these individuals also have a less effective form of acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in slower conversion of acetaldehyde into acetic acid. This combination leads to the accumulation of acetaldehyde after alcohol consumption, causing the alcohol flush reaction and severe, immediate hangover symptoms. Consequently, these individuals are less likely to develop alcoholism. The drug Antabuse (disulfiram) inhibits the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetic acid, producing similar unpleasant effects for drinkers, and has been used in the treatment of alcoholism. Acetaldehyde is also an air pollutant produced by combustion processes, such as automotive exhaust and tobacco smoke. It contributes to the addictive properties of tobacco. Acetaldehyde is toxic, an irritant, and is classified as a probable carcinogen.
